Data-Driven Risk Modelling of Hard Drive Failures for Insurance Pricing

2026-08-20

1. Overview

This report models short-horizon and lifetime hard drive failure risk using a 2021-2022 sample of the Backblaze hard drive dataset (top 15 models by fleet size, ~197k drives, ~127M valid drive-day observations), to inform third-party hard drive insurance pricing. Four research questions are addressed with the module’s core methods - classification, time-series feature engineering, clustering, and regression - with Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional hazards survival analysis used throughout as a supporting tool for handling censoring and cross-validating the core-method findings. See ../README.md for full data provenance, pipeline documentation, and stated assumptions/limitations.

2. Data & Sample

## Drives: 197131 | Models: 15 | Failures observed: 4084 (2.072%)

The fleet is dominated by a small number of failures against a very large population, consistent with hard drives being a genuinely reliable component in aggregate - the central modelling challenge throughout this report is extreme class imbalance, not lack of data volume.

The baseline hazard is low and roughly flat over the short term (survival probability at the 30-day mark, conditional on already having reached that age, is ~0.997) - this is why RQ1/RQ2 use a forward-looking 30-day failure window rather than raw age as the prediction target: age alone carries very little short-horizon signal, so useful prediction has to come from SMART attribute levels and trends. The Cox model shows large, statistically significant hazard ratios across models (e.g. TOSHIBA MG08ACA16TE at ~8.6x the reference model’s hazard), confirming that model identity is a strong risk driver in its own right and motivating the model-level comparisons in RQ3/RQ4. The Schoenfeld residual test rejects strict proportional hazards (expected at this sample size - even small time-varying deviations become statistically significant), a caveat noted for the Cox-based projections in RQ4.

4. RQ1 - Short-Horizon Failure Classification

Can early-life SMART attributes predict whether a drive will fail within the next 30 days, using a snapshot of its current SMART readings?

## Logistic regression AUC: 0.8505
## Elastic-net logistic AUC: 0.7887

Both classifiers substantially beat chance. The plain logistic regression baseline (log1p-transformed, standardized, non-collinear raw SMART predictors) reaches AUC 0.85, slightly ahead of the elastic-net model (AUC 0.79) fit on the full raw+normalized attribute set - regularization handles the collinearity in the fuller feature set well, but doesn’t outperform a carefully preprocessed simpler model here. This is a reasonable, reportable result: SMART snapshots alone carry real short-horizon failure signal, well above the ~50% chance line.

5. RQ2 - Value of Time-Series Features

Do rolling time-series SMART features (7/30-day mean, volatility, and slope) improve on snapshot-only prediction?

Adding rolling features left ranking ability essentially unchanged (AUC 0.791 snapshot-only vs. 0.790 with time-series features added) but improved precision-recall performance (PR-AUC 0.489 -> 0.509). Interpretation: a drive’s current SMART levels already capture most of the information needed to separate failing from healthy drives in a 30-day window; the trend information adds comparatively little extra ranking power, but does help sharpen the precision/recall trade-off - useful for operational decisions (e.g. setting an alert threshold) even though it doesn’t move the headline AUC much.

6. RQ3 - Degradation-Pattern Clustering

Are there distinct clusters of drives with similar degradation trajectories, and do they carry materially different failure risk?

Cluster scatter (PCA projection)

Kaplan-Meier survival by cluster

Failure rate by degradation cluster (k=5, chosen by silhouette score)
cluster n_drives failure_rate
1 51616 0.0113
2 22337 0.0306
3 541 0.6895
4 42146 0.0311
5 11 1.0000

This is the strongest result in the report. K-means on rolling degradation features (silhouette-selected k=5) separates drives into groups with failure rates ranging from ~1.1% (largest, healthy cluster) up to 68.9% and 100% in two small, sharply distinct clusters - a difference of nearly two orders of magnitude. The Cox score test (log-rank-equivalent, robust to the left-truncated time axis used throughout) confirms the survival curves differ across clusters far beyond chance (p < 0.001). Practically: unsupervised degradation patterns alone, with no failure label used in fitting, recover a highly actionable high-risk segment - exactly the kind of signal an insurer would want for risk-based pricing tiers.

Expected loss (failure probability from the per-model Cox survival curve, times a capacity-based replacement-cost proxy) is well explained by coverage length and model identity (R² = 0.81). Coverage length’s linear/quadratic terms are not individually significant once model is in the model - most of the variation is between models, not within a model as coverage grows - while several specific models (ST14000NM001G, ST12000NM0007, TOSHIBA MG08ACA16TE) carry significantly higher expected loss than the reference model at matched coverage length. This is the direct actuarial takeaway: a flat, fleet-wide warranty price would systematically under-price some models and over-price others - the model-level differences here are large enough to justify risk-adjusted pricing tiers rather than a single blended rate.

8. Discussion

Summary of findings. All four RQs point the same direction: hard drive failure risk is predictable well above chance from SMART data (RQ1, AUC 0.85), the predictive signal is concentrated in current attribute levels more than short-term trends (RQ2), degradation patterns cluster into sharply different risk tiers even without using failure labels (RQ3, ~1% vs. ~70-100% failure rate), and that risk difference is large enough to matter financially across models and coverage lengths (RQ4, R² = 0.81 with model identity as the dominant driver). Together this supports a risk-segmented approach to hard drive warranty/insurance pricing - by model at minimum, and potentially by degradation cluster for finer-grained, usage-aware pricing.

Limitations.

  • Observational, enterprise-only population. Backblaze operates data centre workloads; consumer usage patterns (temperature, vibration, power cycling) differ and these results should not be extrapolated to consumer warranty pricing without validation on consumer-representative data.
  • Reduced sample. This analysis uses a 2021-2022, top-15-model subset of the full 2016-2022 Backblaze dataset (see ../README.md) for tractability on commodity hardware; a production deployment would revisit that scoping.
  • SMART attribute coverage varies by manufacturer. Feature engineering was restricted to attributes with broad cross-manufacturer coverage; some vendor-specific signal may have been left out.
  • Correlational, not causal. SMART/degradation associations with failure are statistical associations from observational data, not causal effects.
  • RQ4’s cost proxy ($/TB) is illustrative, not real manufacturer or retail replacement pricing - the loss curves and relative ordering across models are the meaningful output, not the absolute dollar figures.
  • Cox proportional-hazards assumption is formally violated per the Schoenfeld residual test (Section 3), likely reflecting real time-varying risk (e.g. infant-mortality vs. wear-out failure modes) rather than a modelling error; RQ4’s loss projections should be read as first-order approximations, not precise hazard forecasts.
  • Left-truncation is handled via power-on hours as the true age axis (robust to drives already in service before the observation window began), but drive removals for reasons other than failure (e.g. fleet migration) are not distinguishable from failure-free censoring in this dataset.

Ethical and sustainability implications. Risk-based pricing that accurately prices in higher-failure-risk models could, if passed through to manufacturers and consumers, create an incentive to discontinue or avoid lower-reliability models - a plausible reliability-improving effect. It could also concentrate replacement/e-waste incentives around specific models or degradation signatures in ways worth monitoring, and predictive “early-replacement” pricing signals raise a genuine tension between minimizing warranty payouts and encouraging premature hardware replacement (a sustainability cost) versus running drives closer to actual failure (a data-loss risk). Neither is assessed quantitatively here, but both are live considerations were this analysis to inform actual pricing policy.

9. Conclusion

SMART telemetry, engineered through standard analytics techniques (classification, time-series features, clustering, regression) and cross-validated with survival analysis, provides strong, actionable signal for hard drive failure risk at a 30-day operational horizon and over full warranty-length coverage periods. The clearest single finding is RQ3’s degradation clustering, which separates a small, unsupervised high-risk segment carrying failure rates up to two orders of magnitude above the fleet baseline - and RQ4 shows that risk difference is large enough, in expected-loss terms, to justify moving away from flat, fleet-wide warranty pricing toward risk-segmented pricing by model and/or degradation profile.
